title: Peace Be on You: No Faith Kept, No Pledge
intro: Hasan Kamil al-Sayrafi, who edited al-Buhturi's diwan, takes this for a poem of the poet's youth and dates it to about 226 AH (841 CE). It opens with reproach to loved ones who keep no pledge and a stop at the ruins of the Amiri woman's camp, then turns to warnings for the sons of al-Dahhak and for his mother's kin, the sons of Wasil, to pride in his resolve and his sword, and to comfort for a woman weeping at his going. Then comes the passage that made it famous: a night alone in the desert, where he meets a starving wolf, brings it down with two arrows, roasts it and eats a little. It ends with a complaint against fortune and the resolve to seek wealth or die trying. The critic al-Hatimi quoted the wolf passage as among the best things said; al-Kushajim quoted it in his book on hunting and noted that some doubted it was al-Buhturi's, so close is it to the old desert poets in words and themes.

translation: Peace be on you: no faith is kept, and no pledge.
Must you always forsake the ones who love you?
1.sharh: The greeting is a parting one. He reproaches the beloved's people, who keep neither faith nor promise.

translation: My loved ones, parting has kept its promise,
and swiftly, while no promise of yours was ever kept for us.
2.sharh: Parting is pictured as keeping its word, unlike the beloved: separation came on time, while their promises never did.

translation: Ruins of the Amiri woman's home at al-Liwa,
may the rain-stars water your camp: what has become of Hind?
3.sharh: He stops at an abandoned campsite and prays for rain on it, as the old poets did, then asks it for news of Hind, as if the ruins could answer.

translation: Home at al-Liwa, between al-Sarima and al-Hima,
has love no aim but the lingering burn of longing?
4.sharh: Love, he complains, leads nowhere: all it ever arrives at is the slow fire of longing that stays in the heart.

translation: My life for the one whose love has been my torment,
though from that one came no union and no affection.
5.sharh: “My life for him” is the old formula of devotion: the lover offers himself as ransom for the beloved, here one who gave him nothing back.

translation: A beloved among beloveds whom distance has carried off,
and what beloved has distance not come between?
6.sharh: He consoles himself with a general truth: every lover is parted from the beloved in the end.

translation: When you have crossed the desert of al-Ghuwayr, going west,
and left the stony bed of al-Sawajir behind, Sa'd,
7.sharh: He gives a messenger, Sa'd, the road to follow; the message comes in the next line.

translation: tell the sons of al-Dahhak to go gently, for I
am the viper, the deadly snake, the fearless lion.
8.sharh: The message is a warning to a rival clan. He piles up the most dangerous creatures he can name: the viper, the snake no charm can tame, the lion.

translation: Sons of Wasil, go gently: your sister's son
has resolves so firm that even their jests are earnest.
9.sharh: “Your sister's son” is the poet himself: his mother's people are the clan he warns. Even what he decides in jest, he carries through.

translation: Rouse him, and you will rouse nothing but death,
generous youth though he is, whose knots are never untied.
10.sharh: In peace he is open-handed and gracious; roused, he is deadly. “Whose knots are never untied” means that what he binds himself to, a pledge or a purpose, holds.

translation: Fearsome as a sword's blade: if he were hurled
at the peaks of Aja', its heights would sink to hollows.
11.sharh: Hurled at the mountain, he would flatten its peaks into hollows. Aja' is one of the two great mountains in the land of Tayyi', the poet's own tribe.

translation: Men wish that I were one of those
folded away by death, going out neither evening nor morning.
12.sharh: His enemies would like him dead. Going out in the evening and the morning is the ordinary round of the living.

translation: If I did not shoulder the weight of every grave affair
that grieves my enemies, they would not wish what they wish.
13.sharh: Their hatred is the measure of his deeds: he takes on the burdens that harm them, and so they want him gone.

translation: Leave me to them: my resolve will be enough for me
when no spark is struck for him who would end the war.
14.sharh: He speaks to a woman, as the verb shows. A fire-stick that lights is the Arabic image of success; when no peacemaker can manage it and war breaks out, he will need nothing but his own resolve.

translation: I have a companion, keen along its edges, sharp,
with a long baldric, whose edge is never notched.
15.sharh: The companion is his sword. A long baldric means a long blade; in praise of a man the same phrase means he is tall.

translation: Many a woman weeps, lamenting the parting, with tears
that race each other down, like a necklace come apart.
16.sharh: Tears falling one after another are compared to pearls slipping from a broken string, a familiar image in Arabic poetry.

translation: Be sensible: do not grieve that a man of ambition leaves,
who yearns for the heights and has no equal.
17.sharh: He consoles the weeping woman by praising himself: a man of his ambition must travel, and his leaving is no cause for tears.

translation: Whoever is free belongs to resolve and night travel;
the night has its share of his deeds; sleep is a slave.
18.sharh: The free man is set against the slave: he gives his nights to action, and sleep, which rules other men, serves him.

translation: Many a night, when the dawn at its far end
was the last glint of a blade whose sheen the scabbard held,
19.sharh: The first light is a thin edge of steel showing at the mouth of a scabbard; the rest of the dawn is still sheathed in night.

translation: I wrapped it round me while the wolf was drowsing, asleep,
with the eye of a son of the night that knows no sleep.
20.sharh: Even the wolf, proverbial for its wakefulness, is asleep, but the poet is awake with the eye of a night-prowler: “son of the night” could mean a thief.

translation: I start the dusky sandgrouse from their roosts,
and the foxes and grey beasts there grow used to me.
21.sharh: He travels so late and so far that he startles the birds in their sleep, and stays so long in the wilderness that its animals no longer fear him.

translation: Many a grey wolf, filling the eye, his chest
and ribs borne on either side by sturdy legs.
22.sharh: The wolf enters the poem. Atlas, dusky grey, the word for his colour, was used on its own as a name for the wolf.

translation: He has a tail like a well-rope, which he drags,
and a back like the back of a bow, crooked and bent.
23.sharh: Both comparisons come from the desert traveller's own gear: the rope of his water bucket, the bow on his shoulder.

translation: Hunger has folded him till he is twisted hard as rope:
there is nothing in him but bone and breath and hide.
24.sharh: Tawahu al-tawa, “hunger folded him”, is a play on words: the word for hunger comes from folding. The starving wolf is pared down to what keeps him alive.

translation: He clacks his crooked fangs, death in their grooves,
like the chattering teeth of a man shaking with cold.
25.sharh: Even the wolf's threat is drawn from the cold: his jaws work like the teeth of a freezing man.

translation: He made for me, and I was as hungry as he was,
in a waste where no soft living was ever known.
26.sharh: The poet and the wolf are now equals: both starving in a desert with nothing to eat.

translation: There each of us was a wolf, telling himself
of the other; and luck is undone by luck.
27.sharh: Hunger has made the man a wolf too. Only one of them can win, so one's good fortune must be the other's ruin.

translation: He howled, then squatted; I chanted and roused him,
and he came at me like lightning with the thunder behind.
28.sharh: Chanting rajaz verses was what a warrior did before single combat: the poet challenges the wolf like a champion.

translation: I drove into him a wild one, its feathers, you would think,
on a falling star, and the night was black.
29.sharh: The arrow is called by a word used of a wind that blows every way at once; in the dark it streaks like a meteor.

translation: He only grew bolder and fiercer,
and I was sure that he meant it in earnest.
30.sharh: The first arrow does not stop him. The wolf's courage matches the man's.

translation: I sent another after it and sank its head out of sight
where the mind is, and fear, and hate.
31.sharh: The second arrow disappears into the heart, held to be the seat of the mind as well as of fear and hatred. The critic Abdallah al-Tayyib notes that these are a man's qualities, not a wolf's, and wonders whether the wolf stands for some base man.

translation: He fell; I had led him down to death's watering place,
thirsty: if only its water had been sweet.
32.sharh: Death is a watering place: the wolf came to it thirsty for the fight, but the water there is bitter.

translation: I rose, heaped up pebbles and roasted him
on them, the hot ground glowing beneath.
33.sharh: Here the poem parts from the wolf poems of al-Muraqqish and al-Farazdaq, who shared their food with the wolf: al-Buhturi cooks it.

translation: I took a scrap of him, then left him,
and went my way while he lay alone in the dust.
34.sharh: Abdallah al-Tayyib notes how the poet plays down his meal: he took, he says, only a scrap.

translation: The nights have judged us as they would,
and the judgment of time's daughters has no justice.
35.sharh: From the wolf he turns to his own fortunes. Time's daughters are the misfortunes it gives birth to.

translation: Spare me the casting of lots before the night ride:
no ill omen and no good one turns my resolve.
36.sharh: He will not draw lots before a journey; his own resolve decides. The Arabs drew lots with arrow shafts marked “go” and “stay”.

translation: In every calamity I will carry myself
on something like the edge of a sword that India made pure.
37.sharh: Indian steel was the best a sword could be made of. To ride on a sword's edge is to choose the hardest and sharpest course.

translation: so that anyone who fears the night ride, dreading death,
may know there is no turning back God's decree.
38.sharh: If death is decreed, staying at home will not prevent it, so there is no reason to fear the journey.

translation: If I live, praised, then one like me sought riches
to gain wealth, or to have praise of him spread abroad.
39.sharh: He travels for wealth, or for the praise that the generous use of it brings.

translation: If I die without winning, all that is asked of a man
who sets out seeking is to go to the end, and strive.
40.sharh: The poem ends on a principle: a man answers for his effort, not for its outcome.

3.1.3.head: العامِرِيّة
3.1.3.meaning: Al-Amiriyya: a woman of the tribe of Amir; who she was is not known.

3.1.4.head: اللِّوى
3.1.4.meaning: Al-Liwa: where a sand tract thins and bends; here, the name of a place.

3.2.3.head: الأَنواء
3.2.3.meaning: Anwa': the setting and rising of certain stars at dawn, which the Arabs believed brought rain; so, the rains.

3.2.6.meaning: Hind: a woman's name, common in love poetry; who she was is not known.

4.1.4.head: الصَّريمة
4.1.4.meaning: Al-Sarima: “the sand tract”, here a place.

4.1.5.head: الحِمى
4.1.5.meaning: Al-Hima: “the reserve”, pasture closed to grazing; here, a place.

5.1.1.head: نَفس
5.1.1.meaning: “With my life”, that is, I would give my life for the one I love.

7.1.4.head: الغُوَير
7.1.4.meaning: Al-Ghuwayr: a watering place of the tribe of Kalb.

7.2.2.meaning: Batha': a broad stream bed of sand and fine pebbles.

7.2.3.head: السَّواجير
7.2.3.meaning: Al-Sawajir: a river near Manbij, in northern Syria.

8.1.2-3.head: بَنو الضَّحّاك
8.1.2-3.meaning: The sons of al-Dahhak: the kin of al-Hasan ibn Raja' ibn Abi al-Dahhak, whom al-Buhturi satirised in another poem.

8.2.3.head: الصِّلّ
8.2.3.meaning: Sill: a deadly snake that no charm can tame.

9.1.1-2.head: بَنو واصِل
9.1.1-2.meaning: The sons of Wasil: so in the diwan and the recitation. Its editor thinks the right reading is the sons of Wa'il, from whom the Shayban descend, the poet's mother's people.

11.2.2.head: أَجَأ
11.2.2.meaning: Aja': one of the two mountains of the tribe of Tayyi', in northern Arabia.

14.2.6.meaning: Zand: the fire-stick, twirled to make a spark. A stick that lights is success; one that fails, failure.

15.2.2.head: النِّجاد
15.2.2.meaning: Nijad: the baldric a sword hangs from.

19.2.1.meaning: Hushasha: the last remnant of a thing.

19.2.4.head: إِفرِند
19.2.4.meaning: Ifrind: the watered pattern and gleam of a sword's steel; a word from Persian.

20.2.2-3.head: اِبن لَيل
20.2.2-3.meaning: “Son of the night”: one who is awake and abroad at night; the editor glosses it as a thief.

21.1.2.meaning: Qata: sandgrouse, desert birds the size of a pigeon.

21.2.4.head: الرُّبد
21.2.4.meaning: Rubd: “the dusky ones”, a word used of ostriches; the editor glosses it as lions or snakes.

22.1.1.head: أَطلَس
22.1.1.meaning: Atlas: dusky grey; used on its own, a name for the wolf.

24.1.4-5.meaning: “His twisting grew firm”: said of a rope wound tight, and of a man who has grown hard.

27.2.2.head: الجَدّ
27.2.2.meaning: Jadd: luck, fortune. The same letters read jidd mean earnest, as at the end of bayt 30.

28.1.4.head: اِرتَجَزَ
28.1.4.meaning: Rajaz: short chanted verses, the kind a fighter called out before single combat.

29.1.2.head: خَرقاء
29.1.2.meaning: Kharqa': “wild, clumsy”, said of a wind that keeps no direction; here, an arrow.

35.1.5.head: حُكم
35.1.5.meaning: Bi-hukmiha, “as they would”: the diwan and every other source have bi-jawriha, “with their injustice”.

36.1.4.head: القِداح
36.1.4.meaning: Qidah: unfeathered arrow shafts used to draw lots, as the Arabs did before a journey.
